f0039.summary: The end of Morris's cover letter of 4 January 1814, signed in code: the US should keep a force near Florida against the British, and a change in the Regency would help them. Then the start of the proposal he enclosed, whose allegations are its author's: that Jefferson and Madison worked to separate Spain's American colonies, instigated the West Florida insurrection, seized Baton Rouge and encouraged the revolutionaries of Caracas.

1814-04-04_No12.summary: East Florida might be bought on moderate terms, partly paid in produce of the United States, but only with presents or douceurs of perhaps ten thousand dollars; Morris is still waiting at Cadiz for a reply to his proposal.
1814-04-04_No12.en:
Morris to Monroe, Cadiz, 4 April 1814, No. 12 Duplicate. NARA M31 roll 14, frames 82-83; second copy of the cipher, "No 12 Cadiz April 4th Extract", frames 87R-88L. [?word] = inference; [370] = unread group. Spelling follows the code values.

Summary and context: Morris, an unofficial US agent in Spain, reports that East Florida could be bought on moderate terms, partly paid in US produce, but only with about ten thousand dollars in bribes; he is still waiting at Cadiz for a reply to his proposal. Curry (1888) reports the same advice in substance.

1814-04-11_No13.summary: Morris means to go to Madrid shortly, to be nearer the source of authentic information; he has not heard from Monroe since reaching Europe and acts on his own discretion.
1814-04-11_No13.en:
Morris to Monroe, Cadiz, 11 April 1814, No. 13 Duplicate. NARA M31 roll 14, frames 84 and 88L.

Summary and context: Morris, at Cadiz, tells Monroe he will go to Madrid to be nearer reliable information, and that he has had no word from Washington since reaching Europe.

In order to be nearer the sour[?ce] of authentick information and to avail myself of the best means of promoting the objects of my vis[?it] I intend in a short time to proceed to Madrid. Not having had the satisfaction of hearing from you since my arrival in Europe I have been left to the exercise of a discretion on this subject which determines me under present circumstances to proceed. [370] . [370] Anthony Morris

1814-05-11_No14.summary: Detained at Seville on the way to Madrid as the king returns: the fear that he will not take the oath to the constitution; and Morris blames the failure to free the American captives at Algiers on an agent he distrusts.
1814-05-11_No14.en:
Morris to Monroe, Seville, 11 May 1814, No. 14 Triplicate. NARA M31 roll 14, frames 86-87. { } = Morris's own uncoded English; [...] = plain passage omitted here.

Summary and context: Writing from Seville as Ferdinand VII returns, Morris fears the king will not take the oath to the constitution, and blames the failed release of American captives at Algiers on an agent he distrusts. [?Louisiana] needs a slip by Morris (1327 for 1527). Keene went to Algiers in 1814; identifying him as the author meant here is an inference.

I have proceeded this far on my rout to Madrid and am now detained by occurences which render it insecure to proceed and which [?threaten] materially to change the form and views of the Spanish government and politicks.

1814-06-21_No17.summary: After nine pages in clear on the king's return, Morris ends in code: in this unexpected state of things he thinks it best to stay quiet until he hears from Monroe.
1814-06-21_No17.en:
Morris to Monroe, Seville, 21 June 1814, headed No 17 duplicate. NARA M31 roll 14, frames 0107-0111: nine pages in clear, with the date in code at the head of 0107 and three coded lines and the coded signature at the end, on 0111. Read 12 Nov 2026 at the integration of PR #415 with the same key and decoder as the other letters. No contemporary decipherment on the frame. One reader. Only the coded lines are given here; the clear text of the letter is not transcribed.

Summary and context: After a long account in clear of the king's return and the means by which his authority was secured, Morris ends in code: things being as they are, he will stay quiet until he hears from Monroe. The coded heading reads "Seville, June twenty-first, 1814" (read at reduced size).

Conventions: [370] = the unidentified sign that follows full stops. [?word] = inference.

Seville, June twenty-first, 1814.

1814-09-20_No18.summary: The Inquisition restored in July against the wishes of all the ministers, through the king's confessor and the papal nuncio; the Cortes' decrees on the tobacco and other monopolies repealed; arrests, discontent and disturbances at Cadiz; benevolences and forced loans; the king in the arms of the nobility and clergy; no change on Florida and Louisiana; Casa Yrujo reported as the next secretary of state.
1814-09-20_No18.en:
Morris to Monroe, Seville, 20 September 1814, headed No 18 Duplicate. NARA M31 roll 14, frames 0112-0113 (Duplicate, the base text), 0117-0118 (Triplicate) and 0129 (a copy wrongly headed "No 19"; its continuation on 0130 is too dark to read). No contemporary decipherment on these copies. One reader.

Summary and context: Morris reports the restoration of the Inquisition in July, which he says was carried against the wishes of all the ministers through the king's confessor and the papal nuncio; the repeal of the Cortes' decrees on tobacco and other monopolies; arrests, discontent and disturbances at Cadiz; a treasury kept up by forced loans; a king in the hands of the nobility and clergy; no change on Florida and Louisiana; and a report that the Marquis de Casa Yrujo will be the next secretary of state. The coded heading reads "Seville, September twenty, 1814";

1814-10-27_No19.summary: After calling on the Duke de San Carlos on the 13th (page 1, in clear), Morris reports in code that the duke received him without cordiality and has not answered, and that the press and the post office are guarded against anything unfavourable to the government or to Britain and against foreign papers.
1814-10-27_No19.en:
Morris to Monroe, Madrid, 27 October 1814, headed No 19. NARA M31 roll 14: page 1 in clear on 0137 (filmed again on 0138; other copies 0146, 0148); the coded passage on 0139 (base text, left page top), 0147 (Duplicate) and 0149. Catalogue 650 groups 0139 with No. 18; it is the continuation of this letter. No contemporary decipherment on these copies. One reader.

Summary and context: Page 1, in clear, says that with no letters from Washington, and with reports of British troops landing in Florida, Morris came to Madrid to seek talks with the government, arrived on the 9th, and on the 13th called on the Duke de San Carlos to explain his mission. The coded passage says the duke received him coldly and promised an answer he has not given, that the state of opinion is hard to judge, and that the press and the post are policed against anything unfavourable to the government or to Britain.

1814-11-20_Cevallos.summary: The Spanish secretary of state answers Morris: the king resents the conduct of the United States, the appointment of Erving does not repair the refusal to recognise the minister Spain sent in 1809, and satisfaction must begin with that recognition; even so, Morris may deal with Cevallos on matters between the two states.
1814-11-20_Cevallos.en:
(Copy)

My dear Sir — The King my master, to whose knowledge I have [?raised] the paper which you addressed to me under date of the 17th of this month, commands me to answer you that His Majesty keenly resents the conduct which the government of the United States has observed towards the one which, during His Majesty's absence, governed Spain in his royal name. [370] The slight done to His Majesty by the American government in not recognising as minister of Spain the person who was sent with that character to the United States in the year 1809 is not repaired by the appointment which the same States have now made of [?Mr] Erving to reside with the same character near His Majesty.

1814-12-30_No24.summary: From a source he trusts: the Council of State is preparing a report to the king recommending a declaration of war on the United States over Louisiana and Florida; 47,000 soldiers and 5,000 officers back from France, at least 160,000 under arms, and two expeditions of ten thousand fitting out at Cadiz for Mexico and Buenos Aires, to sail early in January.
1814-12-30_No24.en:
Morris to Monroe, Madrid, 30 December 1814, No. 24 (the number and date are in the coded heading). NARA M31 roll 14: top of frame 0220 (base text, clear hand); copies on 0205 (right page, dark film) and 0196 (right page, very dark, with a clerk's decipherment between the lines, transcribed in clerkdecipherment0196.txt). Wholly in code. One reader.

Summary and context: Morris reports, from a source he trusts, that the Council of State is preparing a report to the king recommending a declaration of war on the United States over its conduct on Louisiana and Florida.

1815-01-06_No25.summary: Forwarding Erving's news of the peace (in clear), Morris writes in code that the news, received with great surprise, may change the intended measures of his last letter, that new powers are to be sent to Onis, and that on Erving's instructions he has had no communication with the authorities on it.
1815-01-06_No25.en:
Morris to Monroe, Madrid, 6 January 1815, headed No 25 Duplicate (number and date in clear). NARA M31 roll 14: the coded paragraph is at the foot of frame 0220 and the top of 0221. Another copy on frame 0174 is deciphered in full by a clerk (transcribed in clerkdecipherment0174.txt). One reader.

Summary and context: Morris sends Monroe a copy of a letter from Erving, received that day, with congratulations "on this happy occasion" and the hope that it will "put a stop to the further waste of human blood". Woolfley (2013, Ebook Central p. 106) says Erving's letter was the first report of the peace signed at Ghent to reach Madrid. In code he says the news, received in Madrid with great surprise, may change the "intended measures" of the Spanish government mentioned in his last letter (No.

1815-01-27_No26.summary: The messenger has left with dispatches for Onis, much modified, Morris believes, by the new situation of Spain with the United States after the peace with Great Britain.
1815-01-27_No26.en:
Morris to Monroe, Madrid, 27 January 1815, headed No 26 Triplicate. NARA M31 roll 14, frame 75.

Summary and context: Morris reports that a messenger has left for Onis, the Spanish minister in the United States, and that the peace with Britain has changed Spain's position.

The messenger has at length departed with dispatches for Mr Onis, as intimated in my late letters, but I have grounds to believe much modified by the new situation in which Spain finds herself with the [?United States] in consequence of the peace with [?Great Britain]. Anthony Morris

1815-03-24.summary: No change in relations with Spain; Erving's instructions about the new secretary of legation, Brent, who left Madrid for Valencia; then a long account of discontent under Ferdinand VII: palace favourites, arrests and exiles, the ayuntamientos of 1807 restored, a treasury that cannot pay the army.
1815-03-24.en:
Morris to Monroe, Madrid, 24 March 1815. NARA M31 roll 14, frames 124-125 (Copy A) and 191-193 (Copy B). One reader. The despatch number is unresolved: Copy A's coded heading gives seventeen (1520), Copy B's is overwritten and may begin twenty (873), and the sequence (No 26 on 27 January, No. 29 on 30 May) suggests 27.

Summary and context: Morris reports no change in relations with Spain, quotes Erving on the new secretary of legation, and describes growing discontent under Ferdinand VII, palace favorites, and a treasury unable to pay the army.

Conventions: italic = plain English in the manuscript. [n] = hole. [?word] = inference. Text follows Copy A, using Copy B where A is at fault; every such place is in the collation in reading.md.

(No. [1520 seventeen; number unresolved]) Madrid March 24th 1815.

1815-05-12_No28.summary: Things stand as on 24 March; with no communication with the government since Erving's letters he has had no talks with the secretary of state, but the result at New Orleans must have changed the court's views.
1815-05-12_No28.en:
Morris to Monroe, Madrid, 12 May 1815, headed No 28 Duplicate (number and date in clear). NARA M31 roll 14: frame 0209 right page (Duplicate, the base text) and frame 0210 right page (Triplicate). No contemporary decipherment on these copies. One reader.

Summary and context: Morris writes that things stand as in his letter of 24 March; that with no communication with the government since Erving's letters he has had no talks with the secretary of state, but the result of the expedition against New Orleans must have changed the court's view. In clear he encloses the government's only public document on the return of the "Ex-emperor", says nothing has followed from it but some military appointments (listed at the foot in clear) and that Spain will probably make no move of importance until England's course is known, and notes that he has not heard from Erving since 17 March.

Conventions:

claiborne-1805-10-24.summary: Claiborne reports Spanish troops arriving at Pensacola and ordered to Baton Rouge and Mobile and asks that the forts be strengthened and gunboats stationed (1805); gives the strength of the regular troops at New Orleans and an order of General Wilkinson (January 1806); and writes that a conspiracy injurious to the United States is formed, with persons of high standing concerned (November 1806).

system: The State Department's numerical syllable-and-word code (the JQA table, the = 1385, about 1,600 numbers, rebuilt in ../jqa), in Morris's copy with its sixteen blocks of 100 numbered in reverse order: Morris 100*i + r = JQA 100*(15 - i) + r, each block keeping…
